newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: No time pressure to agree EMU budget pact - Zeitler.
newsitem.headline: No time pressure to agree EMU budget pact - Zeitler.

text.p: Bundesbank council member Franz-Christoph Zeitler said on Wednesday that there was no time pressure on European Union leaders to reach agreement on an EMU budget stability pact at the Dublin summit next month.
Asked by reporters if it was necessary to agree the pact at the meeting on December 13-14, Zeitler said: "There is no pressure of time."

The budget stability pact aims to ensure that countries joining Economic and Monetary Union (EMU) maintain fiscal discipline after they adopt a common currency but the EU's monetary committee has yet to reach an accord on the German-promoted pact.
EU sources said the committee was unable to settle differences over several important aspects of the budget pact after 16 hours of talks on Wednesday.
Zeitler, who was speaking to reporters after addressing the 10th meeting of the European Finance Convention in Dublin, said he hoped progress would be made on the pact at the summit.

But he said he was not sure that the the present draft of the pact provided by the European Commission fully complied with the political will of EU finance ministers as expressed at their informal meeting in Dublin on September 5.
Finance ministers agreed at that meeting that the European Council would impose sanctions against any member state which failed to meet the reference values for their public finances, he said.
This would be necessary to ensure the credibility of the single currency, Zeitler said.
"There must be no doubts from the very outset about the effectiveness and the practical implementation of these sanctions," he said in his speech to the Dublin convention.
"The most important capital which monetary union can accumulate is the trust of the people and the markets in the credibility of its anti-inflation policy foundations."
He also recommended that the European Central Bank target a money supply rather than an exchange rate goal as the basis for its monetary strategy under EMU.
"Gearing monetary policy to the euro's exchange rate against other currencies is ... not a viable option," Zeitler, who is also president of the state central bank in Bavaria, said.
He said the euro curency must itself be a "stability anchor" for other currencies. In addition, the euro must take over the German mark's role as an international investment and reserve currency.
